query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that separates lattice and electronic heat transport will predict that, in defect‐free HfNbTaTiZr, the phonon (lattice) thermal conductivity is nearly temperature invariant between 200 K and 1200 K and is reduced by roughly 30–50% relative to conventional Debye-based estimates, while the electronic thermal conductivity retains a metal-like linear temperature dependence.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk, defect‐free single‐phase HfNbTaTiZr with negligible extrinsic defects, prepared in a controlled environment.
generation.intervention: Application of a predictive framework that decouples lattice and electronic contributions by (a) incorporating effective temperature scaling to capture force-constant and bond-length disorder, and (b) employing separate ab initio-based or ML-enhanced electronic transport models for charge carriers.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted from 200 K to 1200 K in a high-purity, well-characterized sample, ensuring minimal impurity and defect levels.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations arising from atomic size and bonding variations that are captured through an effective temperature parameter.
generation.mechanism: The new model accounts for the static and dynamic lattice distortions that reduce phonon lifetimes and thus lattice thermal conductivity, while treating the electronic conduction using separate, validated metal conduction models. This dual treatment allows the model to avoid conflation of overlapping transport channels observed in conventional approaches.
generation.predicted_outcome: The lattice (phonon) thermal conductivity will remain nearly constant over the specified temperature range and will be significantly lower (by about 30–50%) than values predicted by standard Debye models, whereas the electronic contribution will exhibit a linear increase with temperature, leading to improved overall prediction accuracy of total thermal conductivity.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical estimations that combine lattice and electronic contributions via Debye temperature approximations and do not resolve the complex atomic-scale disorder.
generation.boundary: The prediction is expected to hold for high-purity, single-phase, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr under controlled conditions; deviations might occur if extrinsic defects or phase segregations are present, or outside the 200–1200 K range.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative reduction (i.e. the 30–50% figure) is an estimate based on scaling laws observed in related HEAs; actual deviations may vary, and the separation accuracy is subject to experimental resolution in disentangling the two heat transport channels.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity, defect-free HfNbTaTiZr specimens and measure total thermal conductivity from 200 K to 1200 K using state-of-the-art techniques that separately quantify phonon and electronic contributions (e.g., time-domain thermoreflectance for lattice transport and terahertz spectroscopy for electronic conduction). Compare the independently measured lattice and electronic thermal conductivities with the model predictions.
measurements: Separation of electronic and lattice contributions through the Wiedemann-Franz law (with corrections) or direct measurement methods
Structural characterization (e.g., X-ray/neutron scattering) to validate the degree of lattice distortion
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured lattice thermal conductivity does not exhibit near temperature invariance between 200 K and 1200 K or if its value does not show a reduction on the order of 30–50% relative to conventional Debye-based predictions, then the predictive approach is falsified. Similarly, if the electronic contribution does not follow a predicted linear temperature trend distinct from the lattice behavior, the model must be reconsidered.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the impact of bond length and atomic size disorder on structural and mechanical properties. The resulting lattice distortion plays a pivotal role in various aspects of compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys, as evidenced by prior research (). To isolate the effects of atomic size variations and the resulting lattice distortions on thermodynamic behavior, we intentionally neglect the influence of bond strength or stiffness variations among alloy components. Our approach is rooted in a statistical mechanics treatment of both distortions arising from thermal fluctuations in bond length and those associated with bond length disorder. We explore these phenomena within a simple 2D model and subsequently validate the emergent features within a 3D crystal lattice using MD simulations.

We have also calculated the standard deviation of the nearest-neighbor distances for several experimentally realized HEAs. Specifically, for the FCC Cantor alloy (CoCrMnFeNi), we find Σ=0.0303, and for FCC CoCrCuFeNi, Σ=0.0294 (refer to Table S2 for more details). As previously discussed, bond length disorder effectively elevates the temperature above its actual value. At room temperature, this amounts to an increase of 42% for CoCrMnFeNi and 41% for CoCrCuFeNi (details are available in Table S2). At 1,000 K, the influence of bond length disorder is more modest, effectively raising the temperature by 12% for both alloys. It is crucial to highlight that while bond length disorder significantly impacts thermodynamic properties at lower temperatures, its effect on elastic constants and melting temperatures is much less pronounced. Moreover, these impacts are generally subdued in FCC HEAs owing to their lower levels of local lattice disorder (Σ≤5%) (, ) (see Figs S18 and S23). It is intriguing to observe that one of the classic Hume–Rothery rules posits that stable substitutional solutions exist only when the atomic sizes of the solute and solvent atoms differ by no more than 15% (, ). This implies that there could be an upper bound on the extent of atomic size dispersion allowable in HEAs. The relevance of this rule to HEAs is an open question deserving further investigation; for example, see Ref. (). We should note that in the HEAs we have referenced in Table S2, the maximum value of Σ/l¯ falls below this 15% threshold. We demonstrate that temperature and lattice distortion jointly contribute to numerous thermodynamic, structural, and elastic properties via a unified effective temperature, encompassing both the actual temperature and the extent of lattice distortion. Lattice distortion notably enhances the stability of a single-phase solid solution, as commonly found in binary and multicomponent alloys, by elevating the effective temperature. Increasing temperature further reinforces the stability of a solid solution compared to phase separation or ordering. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide new research avenues for alloy combinations in the periodic table, opening numerous possibilities in novel-alloy applications. However, their electrical characteristics have been relatively underexplored. The challenge in establishing an HEA electrical conductivity model lies in the changes in electronic characteristics caused by lattice distortion and complexity of nanostructures. Here we show a low-frequency electrical conductivity model for the Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. The cocktail effect is found to explain trends in electrical-conductivity changes in HEAs, while the magnitude of the reduction is understood by the calculated plasma frequency, free electron density, and measured relaxation time by terahertz spectroscopy. As a result, the refractory HEA Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin film exhibits both high hardness and excellent conductivity. This combination of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 makes it suitable for applications in atomic force microscopy probe coating, significantly improving their wear resistance and atomic-scale image resolution.
